mcqs.q: Chronic inflammation is best described as:
opts: A prolonged response where injury, inflammation and healing occur simultaneously
A rapid response lasting only hours
mcqs.explain: Chronic inflammation is a prolonged response (weeks–years) in which active inflammation, tissue injury and healing proceed at the same time.

mcqs.q: Compared with acute inflammation, chronic inflammation has a:
opts: More insidious onset and longer duration
mcqs.explain: Chronic inflammation has an insidious onset and long duration, with lymphocytes and macrophages (not neutrophils) and associated fibrosis.

mcqs.q: The hallmark tissue change of chronic inflammation is:
mcqs.explain: Chronic inflammation features connective-tissue proliferation (fibrosis) and angiogenesis, unlike the fluid exudation of acute inflammation.

mcqs.q: Which is a cause of chronic inflammation?
opts: Persistent infection (TB, viral), recurrent acute inflammation, or immune-mediated disease
A single minor cut that heals quickly
mcqs.explain: Chronic inflammation is caused by persistent infections (TB, viral), recurrent/prolonged acute inflammation and immune-mediated disease.

mcqs.q: The cellular infiltrate of chronic inflammation is predominantly:
opts: Mononuclear — lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells
mcqs.explain: Chronic inflammation shows mononuclear infiltration: lymphocytes, macrophages (and plasma cells, eosinophils).

mcqs.q: The DOMINANT cell of chronic inflammation is the:
mcqs.explain: The tissue macrophage is the dominant cellular player in chronic inflammation.

mcqs.q: Tissue macrophages arise from blood monocytes that migrate into tissue within about:
mcqs.explain: Blood monocytes migrate into tissue within about 48 hours of injury and differentiate into tissue macrophages.

mcqs.q: The macrophage of the LIVER is called the:
mcqs.explain: Tissue macrophages have organ-specific names: Kupffer cell (liver), microglia (CNS), alveolar macrophage (lung), histiocyte (connective tissue).

mcqs.q: Microglia are the tissue macrophages of the:
mcqs.explain: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS.

mcqs.q: The macrophages of the LUNG are called:
mcqs.explain: Alveolar macrophages are the tissue macrophages of the lung.

mcqs.q: Proliferative changes in chronic inflammation include:
mcqs.explain: Chronic inflammation stimulates proliferation of small blood vessels (angiogenesis) and fibroblasts, resulting in fibrosis.

mcqs.q: A NON-SPECIFIC chronic inflammation (forming granulation tissue and fibrosis) is exemplified by:
opts: Chronic osteomyelitis or a chronic ulcer
mcqs.explain: Non-specific chronic inflammation (non-specific irritant) gives granulation tissue and fibrosis — e.g. chronic osteomyelitis or chronic ulcer.

mcqs.q: A SPECIFIC chronic inflammation causing a distinctive histologic (granulomatous) response is:
mcqs.explain: Specific chronic inflammation produces a characteristic histologic pattern — e.g. the granulomas of tuberculosis.

mcqs.q: Granulomatous inflammation is characterised by collections of:
opts: Activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with giant cells
mcqs.explain: A granuloma is a collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with Langhans giant cells and a rim of lymphocytes.

mcqs.q: The classic granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis is:
mcqs.explain: Tuberculosis is the classic granulomatous disease, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, showing caseating granulomas.

mcqs.q: In granuloma formation, activated macrophages release IL-12 which:
opts: Activates T cells to release IFN-γ (killing bacteria and recruiting macrophages)
mcqs.explain: Macrophages release IL-12, activating T cells; the IFN-γ they produce kills bacteria and recruits/activates more macrophages.

mcqs.q: Although granuloma formation is protective, it ultimately causes tissue destruction because:
opts: The antigen is poorly digestible and persists
mcqs.explain: The granuloma walls off a poorly-digestible persistent antigen; ongoing inflammation eventually destroys tissue.

mcqs.q: Which cell type is NOT typical of chronic inflammation?
mcqs.explain: Neutrophils dominate acute inflammation; chronic inflammation is dominated by lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells.

mcqs.q: Compared with acute inflammation, chronic inflammation typically:
mcqs.explain: Chronic inflammation is prolonged, lasting weeks, months or years, unlike the hours-to-weeks of acute inflammation.

mcqs.q: Tissue destruction in chronic inflammation is brought about by:
mcqs.explain: Tissue destruction/necrosis in chronic inflammation is caused by the products released by inflammatory cells (e.g. macrophages).

mcqs.q: The large epithelioid-cell-derived multinucleate cells often seen in TB granulomas are:
mcqs.explain: Epithelioid macrophages can fuse into Langhans giant cells, characteristic of tuberculous granulomas.

mcqs.q: Histiocytes are tissue macrophages found in the:
mcqs.explain: Histiocytes are the tissue macrophages of connective tissue/spleen; the brain has microglia and the liver Kupffer cells.

saqs.q: Differentiate acute and chronic inflammation (onset, cells, hallmark).
saqs.a: Acute: rapid onset, neutrophils, fluid exudation. Chronic: insidious onset, lymphocytes/macrophages, fibrosis.

saqs.q: List the causes of chronic inflammation.
saqs.a: Persistent infection (TB, viral), recurrent/prolonged acute inflammation, and immune-mediated disease.

saqs.q: Name the cells of chronic inflammation and the dominant one.
saqs.a: Mononuclear cells: lymphocytes, macrophages (dominant), plasma cells, eosinophils.

saqs.q: Give the organ-specific names of tissue macrophages.
List the three characteristics of chronic inflammation.
Define granulomatous inflammation and give the classic example.
saqs.a: A chronic pattern with collections of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) ± giant cells. Classic example: tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), with caseation.

saqs.q: Outline the immune mechanism of granuloma formation.
saqs.a: Activated macrophages release IL-12 → activate T cells → IFN-γ → kills bacteria and recruits/activates more macrophages.
